{{Short description|Equations describing traffic rate}}
In [[queueing theory]], a discipline within the mathematical [[probability theory|theory of probability]], '''traffic equations''' are equations that describe the mean arrival rate of traffic, allowing the arrival rates at individual nodes to be determined. Mitrani notes "if the network is stable, the traffic equations are valid and can be solved."<ref name="mitrani">{{Cite book | doi = 10.1017/CBO9781139173087.005| chapter = Queueing networks| title = Probabilistic Modelling| pages = 122–155| year = 1997| last1 = Mitrani | first1 = I. | isbn = 9781139173087}}</ref>{{rp|125}}

==Jackson network==
In a [[Jackson network]], the mean arrival rate <math>\lambda_i</math> at each node ''i'' in the network is given by the sum of ''external'' arrivals (that is, arrivals from outside the network directly placed onto node ''i'', if any), and ''internal'' arrivals from each of the other nodes on the network. If external arrivals at node ''i'' have rate <math>\gamma_i</math>, and the routing matrix<ref>As explained in the [[Jackson network]] article, jobs travel among the nodes following a fixed routing matrix.</ref> is ''P'', the traffic equations are,<ref name="harrison">{{Cite book | last1 = Harrison | first1 = Peter G. | authorlink = Peter G. Harrison | last2 = Patel | first2 = Naresh M. | title = Performance Modelling of Communication Networks and Computer Architectures | publisher = Addison-Wesley | date = 1992 | isbn = 0-201-54419-9 | url-access = registration | url = https://archive.org/details/performancemodel0000harr }}{{Page needed|date=December 2010}}</ref> (for&nbsp;''i''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1,&nbsp;2,&nbsp;...,&nbsp;''m'')

::<math>\lambda_i = \gamma_i + \sum_{j=1}^m p_{ji}\lambda_j.</math>

This can be written in matrix form as

::<math>\lambda(I-P)=\gamma \, , </math>

and there is a unique solution of unknowns <math>\lambda_i</math> to this equation, so the mean arrival rates at each of the nodes can be determined given knowledge of the external arrival rates <math>\gamma_i</math> and the matrix ''P''. The matrix ''I''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''P'' is surely non-singular as otherwise in the long run the network would become empty.<ref name="mitrani" />

==Gordon–Newell network==
In a [[Gordon–Newell theorem|Gordon–Newell network]] there are no external arrivals, so the traffic equations take the form (for&nbsp;''i''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1,&nbsp;2,&nbsp;...,&nbsp;''m'')

::<math>\lambda_i = \sum_{j=1}^m p_{ji} \lambda_j.</math>
